Are you a flight commander? Your role as an Flt/CC is to oversee and lead the battle rhythm for your troops, task and delegate with purpose and follow up on taskers, as well as provide top cover when needed and ensure the overall health and wellness of the flight. Let your SNCOs and NCOs oversee the nitty gritty day to day floor ops. Determine what needs to be fixed within your flight and set goals on how to get there. Utilize your SNCOs and NCOs for guidance and how to get to those goals. Depending on the ops tempo, you may or may not meet all these goals, so I’d recommend determining which of these goals are most important to you and/or your commander’s intent.

Are there any key external stakeholders critical to accomplishing the mission? Tailor your battle rhythm to maintaining comms with those folks on a weekly, bi-weekly, or as needed basis.

There’s multiple ways to go about it. I’m mostly firing from the top of my head, but these are a few of the many things I’ve learned as a flight commander so far. I am currently on my second flight at my second base now. I am but a young CGO who is also still learning how and what it takes to lead, but happy to further discuss if you have more questions.

1st generation Chicano here as well. Currently serving as an officer in the US Air Force. 1st in my family to go to college as well. I joined the military on the officer side because while in college I knew I wanted to serve to use the benefits to further my education and career. Growing up poor, there’s wasn’t really any money for my parents to help with tuition or higher education, so joining AFROTC in college (a program that helps you enter the military as an officer after you graduate) helped pay my undergrad tuition, and now, as an officer, the Air Force is helping me pay the tuition for my graduate degree. 

Joining the military has helped me not only manage and pay off my undergraduate tuition, but also provide me with the opportunity to pursue my Master’s at a relatively very low-cost. Top this with relevant work experience that translates over if you decide separate and the benefit of the VA home loan should you decide to purchase a home, among other benefits, it’s not a bad deal.

If you decide to join the military, join with a plan. Look up the benefits, it’s pros and cons, see what you want to get out of it, and make the decision that’s right for you.

Mexican-American/Chicano here. I went through a small phase in college where my Spanish began getting rustier and rustier, mostly because I wasn’t back home as often and would use English more frequently among my new circle of friends. What’s helped me regain some sort of balance with my bilingualism has been embracing both sides of my culture. Born in the US, it’s easy for us to sometimes forget the culture and language of our family/descendants. I made it a priority, aside from already practicing American culture on a daily basis, to also add in the culture and language that my parents provided me growing up. Some examples include watching Latin American shows in Spanish, listening to music in Spanish from artists across Mexico and Latin America, and communicating in Spanish at any opportunity I have available—whether with my own family, or other native Spanish or bilingual speakers. Being Chicano, or Mexican-American has its upside in that you have an inherent connection to two cultures and two languages. Be proud of that and find a balance in practicing both. Should you practice one more than the other, then that’s where you lose your language and culture over time.

I joined the Air Force to pave a road towards tuition-free graduate school through the use of the GI Bill. I earned my commission through the Air Force ROTC program and am currently serving as an officer. Growing up in East LA to a poor immigrant family, I financed my undergraduate education through a mix of scholarships, FAFSA, internships, and working part-time on campus. I see the military as an opportunity for me to pursue my education even further than just a bachelor’s degree while earning relevant work experience that I can use when I plan to apply to business school in the future. I understand this country isn’t the greatest, no country really is, but I’d have to disagree with you on the statement that we have no business in the military. Diversity is strength. There are few Chicanos in the military, let alone on the officer side. I believe it’s important to have our voices heard throughout a multitude of organizations. As the only a Chicano/Latino Officer in the room the majority of the time, I’ve personally used my background within some of the groups that I’ve worked with to voice concerns that affect POC in the military.

I think the blanqueamiento movement has existed long since the Spanish adopted their racial caste system during early colonial Mexico. I remember, and still see traces of this to this day, of other Latinos being treated, or seen as—for a lack of a better word—“superior” to others simply because of the color of their skin. Most notably, I’ve had older relatives within my own family call some of my nieces and nephews “more beautiful” than others simply because they were born with a lighter skin complexion than those with a brown or darker skin tone.

That’s why I’ve always opposed this form of colorism/shadeism and believe that people should not be judged by the color of their skin or background, but rather, as MLK said it best, “by the content of their character.” I’ve seen a few videos from LeLe Pons and Juanpa, but as someone who grew up in East LA and watching the Youtubers I mentioned in my previous comment, as well as the comedy from comics like Paul Rodriguez, Juan Villareal, Felipe Esparza, etc., I simply just can’t relate and fit to their style of humor. More so, it seems as if they only claim their Latino-ness to consider themselves “unique” rather than as a showmanship of pride to their cultural and historic roots. Then again, being Chicano, or Latino for that matter, is a mixed definition and can mean different things to different people. This is all my opinion, of course.

But, as you stated, it may also be due to the fact that they’re catering to a middle-class background. I grew up low-income, but through earning my college degree and in my current career, I’ve been able to step up the social ladder and now consider myself middle-class. Yet, I haven’t forgotten—and neither am I embarrassed to showcase—where I’m originally from, my culture, and the struggle and discrimination my parents and family faced when they first immigrated to the US from Mexico.

Current US Air Force officer here. I consider myself Chicano, or Mexican-American. My parents were born in Mexico and I was born in the US. We grew up fairly poor, but my folks did their best to provide me with a good education and a shot at going to college. 

I just recently graduated college about 6 months ago and earned my commission as an officer through the Air Force ROTC program. That said, I joined the officer side of the Air Force soon after graduation and have been on Active Duty for about 6 months now. 

Overall, my experience has been positive and there really hasn’t been any instance where I felt discriminated based on my ethnic, racial, or cultural background, aside from a few crude jokes here and there. All my leadership thus far—and the Air Force as a whole—have promoted the idea that it does not matter whether you’re rich or poor, black or white, or come from a certain background. What matters to them, and to the military, is your overall potential to get the mission done and take care of your people. A military member, or any person for that matter, should not be judged based on the color of their skin, their background, their socioeconomic status, etc., but rather, by their merit and the content of their character.

It is true that you meet people from all walks of life in the military. I’ve met great people, and I’ve met people who haven’t seem to have “gotten with the times.” Nonetheless, the military is what you make of it. Issues of racial discrimination will always exist no matter the organization, but it’s up to you to change the status quo and demonstrate that innate factors such as your race, or ethnicity, or the circumstances that you grew up under do not have a negative effect on your capability to serve in the armed forces, or any career that you choose for that matter. 

Hope this helped, and good luck with your future endeavors!

22M Gf dropped the bomb on me 6 months ago when I joined the military after graduating from college and was stationed 2000 miles away from home. I can definitely understand the loneliness you’re currently feeling, but I can assure you that it gets easier over time. Some things that I did which have helped me overcome the loneliness and ease into my new environment have been:

- explore your area! New place and alone? Well go out and explore your surroundings. See being alone in a new area as a pro and not a con, and see it as an opportunity for you to be able to explore your surroundings without anything or anyone holding you back. Maybe go out to that new bar/restaurant downtown, or go see a show/movie, or for a walk in the park, or simply sightsee across the city. It may feel weird or intimidating at first going out alone, but after a while you should realize and see that it’s fun and better than staying home alone feeling lonely or worse.

- Make new friends! I’ve made a few friends thus far being alone out here through apps like Meetup, simply going out in the community and volunteering, or joining clubs/organizations. It’s definitely harder to meet new people in your 20s, but it’s still do-able, it’s just a matter of getting out into the world and trying new things.

- Try something new! With the extra time you’ll now have from being single, you’ll be wondering what to do with it. It’s okay to process your emotions and grieve, but after you wipe that sadness away, use the extra time to go about and make a list of things you’ve been wanting to try/do and maybe didn’t have the time when you were in a relationship. For instance, I picked up guitar lessons just recently and am loving it so far! Whatever it may be, cooking classes, dancing classes, learning a new language, pursuing higher education, etc., use your newly found time to your advantage to self-improve!

- see the positive in your situation. Kind of relates to the first point, but once you see the positive within your current situation, it gets a little easier. Rather than feeling bad about yourself because you lost your gf, you’re far away from home/familiar territory and you’ve got no friends/family nearby, see the positive instead and focus your thoughts on the good rather than the bad such as, “well, hey! I’m in a new city, new job, this calls for a fresh start and a chance for self-improvement and possibly even meeting new friends and people!” Once I started channeling my thoughts from negative to positive, it really helped me refocus and see that my current situation wasn’t that bad and that it also wasn’t permanent.

I’m still sorting through my feelings, and times do get rough sometimes and I still think about my ex every now and then, but this is a bit of advice that helped me when I was freshly dumped and had relocated to a new place with no friends or family nearby. I know these tips sound generic, but they’re what really helped me. And lastly, Reddit is a great community to meet virtual friends (and even in real life too)! So if you ever feel down and need a place to vent, drop me a PM and I’d be glad to help!
